frameworks.name: The Big Three Partnership Inputs
frameworks.definition: A partnership creates value only when at least one partner contributes something the other lacks: knowledge, money, or time. If both partners have identical inputs on all three axes, one partner is unnecessary.

frameworks.name: Mission-Values-Interests Alignment
frameworks.definition: A durable partnership requires alignment on three levels: where the business goes (mission), how it gets there (values), and whether lifestyle/interests are compatible. Misalignment on any axis creates persistent conflict.

claims.text: If both partners possess the same knowledge, money, and time, one partner is unnecessary and both give away half their equity for zero incremental benefit to the business.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Identical inputs across all three partnership dimensions create no complementary skill leverage.

claims.text: A partnership only creates value if the partner fills a capability gap the founder genuinely cannot fill alone—a need does not justify equity as compensation.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Equity is the highest-cost currency in a business; reserving it for true complementary inputs maximizes retained ownership for growth.
bounded_by: Does not apply when hiring someone for a specific skill (e.g., an accountant); pay for the service instead of giving equity.

claims.text: Written agreements are essential in partnerships, not because they enable lawyer involvement, but because they facilitate difficult conversations about expectations before stakes exist, and ensure shared understanding of roles.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Explicit written expectations clarify misaligned assumptions early, before resentment or financial loss compounds.
bounded_by: The purpose is clarity and dialogue, not to bring lawyers into disputes; write contracts with the intention of never needing to consult them.

claims.text: If one partner does a disproportionate amount of work at the outset, the other partner will resent them later; conversely, if one partner extracts maximum value from an overworked partner, the overworked partner will resent them and renegotiate.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Inequitable work distribution creates resentment; to prevent renegotiation later, the person with leverage should give more, not take more, to establish reciprocity norms.

claims.text: When business partners are in a marriage-like relationship, their personal life (financial habits, reliability, decision-making patterns) will inevitably spill into the business, creating systemic instability if misaligned.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Personal unreliability creates business unreliability because partners share operational exposure and reputational risk.
bounded_by: Does not apply to transactional vendor relationships; applies only to equity partnerships with shared liability.

claims.text: Misalignment on mission (where to take the business), values (how to operate), or interests (lifestyle compatibility) guarantees persistent conflict; the easiest test is whether both partners would make the same decision when presented with identical data.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Aligned decision-making frameworks prevent costly renegotiations and strategic conflicts that erode trust.
bounded_by: Does not apply when partners deliberately seek diverse perspectives for a specific trade-off benefit.

claims.text: Partners must have complementary skill sets but aligned mission, values, and interests; attempting to partner with someone who is identical in skills but different in core worldview is a structural recipe for failure.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Complementary skills reduce duplication and enable leverage; aligned values enable shared decision-making under uncertainty.

claims.text: People avoid writing partnership agreements not because of genuine disagreement with the practice, but because they don't want to have hard conversations; this avoidance is a reliable predictor that they will fail to communicate when stakes are high.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: Communication difficulty in the low-stakes agreement phase predicts communication failure in high-stakes disputes.

claims.text: You want to be proud to associate with your business partner—not merely okay with them—because you will be presenting them to stakeholders, clients, and team members as a reflection of the business itself.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: A partner's public reputation compounds directly into the business's reputation; shame or embarrassment about association signals misalignment.

claims.text: If you need something done (e.g., an accountant's knowledge), the solution is to pay for that skill as a service, not to grant equity; equity must be reserved for partners who drive growth.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
conditions: Skill shortage or service need identified
claims.mechanism: Equity dilutes ownership too severely for transactional value; paying for services preserves upside for growth-driving partners.

claims.text: Most people fail to think 10 years into the future when building partnerships or businesses, which is why most businesses remain small; thinking long-term about partner contribution is a prerequisite for scaling.
claims.speaker: Alex Shamosi
claims.mechanism: 10-year forward thinking reveals which partners will remain valuable contributors as the business grows; short-term thinking leads to equity dilution with low-growth partners.

examples.text: Alex Shamosi describes being told early in his entrepreneurial career by someone that they would only do business on a handshake because they trusted the person. Shamosi rejected this philosophy, realizing that banks don't lend money on handshakes and that insisting on unwritten agreements is an unusual position. He now writes contracts with the explicit intention of using them as vehicles for dialogue about difficult topics, not as instruments to invoke lawyers later.

Two potential business partners want to take the same company in different strategic directions: one wants to go one way, the other wants to go another way. When asked what they should do, Shamosi's response is either figure it out or one of you shouldn't be here—demonstrating that hidden mission misalignment is a structural blocker that must be surfaced immediately.

practices.text: Document partnership expectations in writing and ensure they are equitable and well-understood by both parties before any money or equity changes hands.
Test partnership fit by presenting both partners with the same data and asking whether they would make the same decision; if they wouldn't, relationship risk is high.

Before entering a partnership, clearly identify which of the three inputs (knowledge, money, time) each partner brings that the other lacks; if there is no clear differentiation, question whether equity is warranted.

When one partner has leverage in the early stage (e.g., availability, work ethic, capital), voluntarily offer more value than contractually required to establish reciprocity and prevent future renegotiation.
Evaluate a potential partner not just on professional qualifications but on lifestyle stability, financial habits, and decision-making patterns, as these will inevitably affect the business.
